question: What does “Big Ben” technically refer to?
note: Big Ben is the nickname of the Great Bell. The tower itself has been called Elizabeth Tower since 2012.

question: What is the usual nickname for the London Underground?
note: Londoners have called the Underground “the Tube” for well over a century.

question: Which English city is famous for its Roman baths?
note: Bath grew around hot springs used by the Romans, who called the settlement Aquae Sulis.

question: Where is the Giant’s Causeway?
note: The basalt columns of the Giant’s Causeway are on the north coast of County Antrim in Northern Ireland.

question: In which English county is Stonehenge?
note: Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire.

question: Loch Ness is in which part of the UK?
note: Loch Ness is a long freshwater loch in the Scottish Highlands.

question: 10 Downing Street is most closely associated with which office?
choices: The Speaker of the House of Commons
note: 10 Downing Street is the official residence and office of the UK prime minister.

question: Robin Hood is traditionally associated with which forest?
note: The Robin Hood legends are especially associated with Sherwood Forest in Nottinghamshire.

question: Which theatre is most closely associated with Shakespeare’s company in London?
note: Shakespeare’s company performed at the Globe Theatre, first built on the south bank of the Thames in 1599.

question: The Brown family meet a bear at a London railway station and name him after it. Which station?
note: The Browns first meet him at Paddington station, which is where he gets his name.

question: Which city is most closely associated with the Beatles’ beginnings?
note: The Beatles formed in Liverpool, and the city remains central to the band’s history.

question: In what year was the Battle of Hastings?
note: The Battle of Hastings was fought in 1066 and led to the Norman conquest of England.

question: Who defeated Harold II at the Battle of Hastings?
note: William, Duke of Normandy, won the battle and became William I, commonly called William the Conqueror.

question: In which year was Magna Carta first sealed?
note: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215.

question: The Gunpowder Plot took place in which year?
note: The plot to blow up Parliament was uncovered in 1605.

question: What was Guy Fawkes found guarding beneath the House of Lords?
note: Fawkes was discovered with the gunpowder prepared for the plot, which is why his name became so closely tied to it.

question: Which two houses fought the Wars of the Roses?
note: The dynastic conflict is conventionally associated with the houses of Lancaster and York.

question: How many wives did Henry VIII have?
note: Henry VIII had six wives: Catherine of Aragon, Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard, and Catherine Parr.

question: Who was the mother of Elizabeth I?
note: Elizabeth I was the daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn.

question: Which Scottish king became James I of England after Elizabeth I died?
note: James VI of Scotland also became James I of England in 1603, joining the crowns under one monarch.

question: In what year did the Great Fire of London begin?
note: The Great Fire began in September 1666 and burned through much of the old City of London.

question: Which monarch gave her name to the Victorian era?
note: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901, and the period is commonly called the Victorian era.

question: The people often called “Beefeaters” at the Tower of London are officially known as what?
note: “Beefeater” is the familiar nickname for the Yeoman Warders of His Majesty’s Royal Palace and Fortress the Tower of London.

question: In Arthurian legend, whose sword is Excalibur?
note: Excalibur is King Arthur’s famous sword in the Arthurian tradition.

question: In the famous story of King Cnut and the tide, what is the king trying to demonstrate?
choices: That the sea belongs to the crown
note: In the traditional account, Cnut’s failed command to the tide is used to show the limits of earthly royal power and rebuke flattering courtiers.

question: Bonfire Night is observed on which date?
note: Bonfire Night, also called Guy Fawkes Night, is held on 5 November.

question: Boxing Day falls on which date?
note: Boxing Day is 26 December in the UK and several other countries.

question: Pancake Day in Britain is another name for what?
note: Pancake Day is the common British name for Shrove Tuesday, the day before Ash Wednesday.

question: Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?
note: Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice was published in 1813.

question: Ebenezer Scrooge appears in which Dickens work?
note: Scrooge is the central character of Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol.

question: Who created Sherlock Holmes?
note: Arthur Conan Doyle introduced Sherlock Holmes in A Study in Scarlet in 1887.

question: Hercule Poirot was created by whom?
note: Agatha Christie created the Belgian detective Hercule Poirot.

question: Who wrote The Woman in White?
note: Wilkie Collins published The Woman in White in serial form beginning in 1859.

question: Who wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four?
note: George Orwell’s dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four was published in 1949.

question: Who created James Bond?
note: Ian Fleming introduced James Bond in the 1953 novel Casino Royale.

question: Who plays Mr Bean?
note: Rowan Atkinson created and plays the largely silent comic character Mr Bean.

question: In Doctor Who, what does TARDIS stand for?
choices: Time And Relative Dimension In Space
Travel Across Real Dimensions In Space
Time And Reality Device In Space
Temporal And Relative Distance In Space
note: TARDIS stands for Time And Relative Dimension In Space.

question: What was Monty Python’s television sketch show called?
note: Monty Python’s Flying Circus first aired on the BBC in 1969.

question: The theatrical term “Pinter pause” takes its name from which playwright?
note: The phrase refers to the distinctive use of pauses and silences associated with Harold Pinter’s plays.

question: Doctor Who was first broadcast on the BBC in which decade?
note: The first episode of Doctor Who was broadcast on 23 November 1963.

question: In “bangers and mash,” what are the bangers?
note: Bangers and mash is a dish of sausages served with mashed potatoes, often with gravy and onions.

question: Traditional shepherd’s pie is made with which meat?
note: Shepherd’s pie traditionally uses lamb or mutton. The beef version is usually called cottage pie.

question: Haggis is especially associated with which country?
note: Haggis is strongly associated with Scottish cuisine and with Burns Night suppers.

question: What is inside the sausage-meat coating of a Scotch egg?
note: A Scotch egg consists of a cooked egg wrapped in sausage meat and coated in breadcrumbs.

question: A traditional cream tea usually includes scones with what?
note: Scones, clotted cream, and jam are the core of a cream tea; Devon and Cornwall famously differ over which topping goes on first.

question: Which of these would be least typical on a full English breakfast?
note: A full English commonly includes items such as eggs, bacon, sausages, beans, tomatoes, mushrooms, and toast; a croissant belongs to a different breakfast tradition.

question: Which food is famously associated with spectators at Wimbledon?
note: Strawberries and cream are one of Wimbledon’s best-known traditions.

question: Under the modern Laws of Cricket, how many legal deliveries are in an over?
note: An over consists of six legal deliveries.

question: The annual Boat Race is traditionally contested by which two universities?
note: The Boat Race is the long-running rowing contest between Oxford and Cambridge.

question: The Ashes is a cricket series between England and which country?
note: The Ashes is the historic Test cricket rivalry between England and Australia.
